paragraphs.heading: Songs and calls
paragraphs.text: Bird sounds come in two broad kinds, songs and calls. Ornithologists tell them apart by how complex they are, how long they last and when they are used. A song is the longer, more elaborate sound, tied to holding ground and to courtship and mating. A call is simpler and does jobs such as raising an alarm or keeping a flock in touch. Not everyone draws the line the same way: some experts sort sounds by their purpose, so even short pigeon sounds or the drumming of a woodpecker count as song.

paragraphs.heading: The syrinx
paragraphs.text: In mammals the larynx sits at the top of the windpipe, or trachea. A bird instead has a bony voice organ, the syrinx, down at the trachea's lower end. The bird forces air past membranes, which make sound waves, and the syrinx, sometimes with an air sac around it, resonates to them. Changing the tension on the membranes shifts the pitch, while breathing out harder or softer changes both pitch and loudness. The bird can work the two sides of the trachea separately, which lets some species sound two notes at the same moment.

paragraphs.heading: Winning a mate
paragraphs.text: One of the two main jobs of song is to attract a partner. Experiments suggest that how well a bird sings may be a good sign of its fitness. Parasites and illness can change features such as how often a bird sings, so song can be a trustworthy clue to health. In some species the number of different songs a bird knows, its repertoire, also seems to reflect fitness. A female may therefore pick a male by the quality of his singing and the size of his repertoire.

paragraphs.heading: Holding ground
paragraphs.text: The other main job is defending a territory. Territorial birds trade songs to work out where one territory ends and the next begins. Because song may honestly show a bird's quality, rivals may be able to judge each other and skip a fight that would cost a lot of energy. More complex songs are taken as a bigger threat. Some birds answer a rival by singing back the very same song type, which may be an aggressive signal, though the evidence is mixed.

paragraphs.heading: Who does the singing
paragraphs.text: Outside the tropics in Eurasia and the Americas, nearly all song comes from males. In the tropics, and even more in the desert belts of Australia and Africa, females usually sing as much as males do. The usual explanation is the irregular climate of those dry regions, where birds must breed whenever conditions turn good. When breeding has no fixed season, both partners must be brought into breeding condition, and singing together in duets helps do that. More than 400 bird species are known to duet.

paragraphs.heading: Music without a voice
paragraphs.text: Some birds barely use their voices at all. Storks, for instance, make rhythmic sounds by clattering their bills. Males of some manakins have evolved several ways of making mechanical sounds, including one resembling a method certain insects use. Charles Darwin called sounds like these instrumental music, and more recently they have been called sonation. The word covers deliberate signals made with the bill, wings, tail, feet or body feathers rather than the syrinx.
